entity.name: Salvador Dali
entity.description: The showman of Surrealism who painted melting clocks and cultivated madness as method. Dali mastered classical technique then weaponized it for the subconscious, producing The Persistence of Memory and co-writing Un Chien Andalou with Bunuel. His flamboyant mustache became as famous as his art.

story.name: Salvador Dali
story.description: Born in the shadow of a dead brother in Figueres, expelled from art school in Madrid, painting melting clocks in Paris, fleeing to America, and returning to build a museum in his hometown theatre.

moments.name: Salvador Dali Is Born Nine Months After His Identically Named Brother Dies
moments.subtitle: His parents give him a dead boy's name, and the ghost haunts his art for life
moments.description: On 11 May 1904, Salvador Dali was born at Carrer Monturiol 20 in Figueres, Catalonia, Spain. His older brother, also named Salvador, had died of gastroenteritis on 1 August 1903 at age one. Dali's parents gave their new son the same name, and young Salvador grew up visiting his brother's grave, where a headstone bore his own name. Dali later said his dead brother was probably the first version of himself but conceived too much in the absolute. The ghost of this brother haunted Dali's art throughout his career, appearing in works like Portrait of My Dead Brother (1963).

moments.name: A 22-Year-Old Dali Visits Paris and Meets His Idol Picasso
moments.subtitle: The young Catalan arrives at the master's studio with paint under his fingernails and ambition to spare
moments.description: In April 1926, 22-year-old Salvador Dali made his first trip to Paris, where he met Pablo Picasso, the artist he most revered. Picasso had already heard favorable reports about Dali from fellow Catalan Joan Miro. The meeting proved formative: over the next few years, Dali produced works strongly influenced by both Picasso and Miro before developing his own distinctive Surrealist style. Dali had recently left the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Madrid shortly before his final exams, confident his technical mastery already surpassed what the school could teach him. The Paris trip marked Dali's entry into the international avant-garde.

moments.name: Dali Paints The Persistence of Memory and Becomes Surrealism's Star
moments.subtitle: A canvas of melting pocket watches becomes the most recognized Surrealist painting ever made
moments.description: In August 1931, Salvador Dali completed The Persistence of Memory, a small oil painting measuring just 24 by 33 centimeters, depicting soft melting watches draped across a barren landscape inspired by the Catalan coast. Dali had officially joined the Surrealist group in Paris in 1929, where Andre Breton hailed his work as the most hallucinatory produced up to that time. Dali developed what he called the paranoiac-critical method to channel subconscious imagery into precise, hyperrealistic paintings. The Persistence of Memory became the defining image of the Surrealist movement and now hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

moments.name: Dali and Bunuel Release Un Chien Andalou, Surrealism's Most Shocking Film
moments.subtitle: A 17-minute film opening with a razor slicing an eyeball scandalizes Paris and launches two careers
moments.description: In 1929, Salvador Dali collaborated with filmmaker Luis Bunuel on Un Chien Andalou (An Andalusian Dog), a 17-minute short film that became Surrealism's most infamous cinematic work. Dali's main contribution was co-writing the script, which the pair built from their dreams. The film's opening sequence, showing a razor blade slicing through a woman's eye, remains one of cinema's most disturbing images. The film had no conventional plot, instead juxtaposing dreamlike sequences of dead donkeys on pianos and severed hands. It was a commercial hit in Paris, running for eight months. Un Chien Andalou helped establish both Dali and Bunuel as leading Surrealists.

moments.name: Salvador Dali Dies Inside the Museum He Built in His Hometown Theatre
moments.subtitle: The showman spends his final years as a recluse in the tower of his own artistic monument
moments.description: On 23 January 1989, Salvador Dali died of heart failure at age 84 in the Torre Galatea, a tower attached to the Dali Theatre-Museum in Figueres, Spain. The museum, which Dali had built inside the ruins of the old Municipal Theatre where he held his first exhibition at age 14 in 1918, had opened in 1974 and was his greatest late-career creation. Dali spent his final years as a near-recluse in the tower after his wife Gala's death in 1982. Per his wishes, Dali was buried in the crypt beneath the museum's stage. The Theatre-Museum remains Spain's second-most-visited museum after the Prado.
